Load Libraries

{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(lawstat)

Load the Data

{r}
# load the state file
data = read.csv('iran_war_gas_prices_by_state.csv')

Basic EDA

Data Structure

{r}
# structure and size
names(data)
str(data)
head(data)
dim(data) # 50 rows 9 columns

The file has 50 rows and 9 columns, one row per state. Two columns are text labels (state and region), one names the source, and six are numbers: three dated prices, the dollar increase, the percent increase, and the gap from the national average.

Data Quality

{r}
# missing values per column
sum(colSums(is.na(data))) # 0
sum(duplicated(data$state)) # 0

No missing values and no state shows up twice.

Data Preparation

Change Names

{r}
# short names for the columns we use
data$prewar = data$gas_price_prewar_feb27
data$mar19 = data$gas_price_mar19_2026
data$jan08 = data$gas_price_jan08_2026
data$increase = data$price_increase_since_war
data$pct = data$pct_increase_since_war

Compare Columns

{r}
# check the increase columns against the prices
max(abs(data$increase - (data$mar19 - data$prewar))) # 6.661338e-16
max(abs(data$pct - 100 * data$increase / data$prewar)) # 0.04964539

The dollar increase matches the March 19 price minus the Feb 27 price. The percent increase matches to within 0.05 percentage points. So both columns are correct.

Change Region to a Category

{r}
# region as a category
data$region = factor(data$region)
table(data$region)

The four regions have 12, 11, 14, and 13 states, so the groups are close in size.

Add Predictors

{r}
# price change before the war jan 8 to feb 27
data$pre_trend = data$prewar - data$jan08

# coastal states typed as a short list
coast = c('Maine', 'New Hampshire', 'Massachusetts', 'Rhode Island', 'Connecticut',
          'New York', 'New Jersey', 'Delaware', 'Maryland', 'Virginia',
          'North Carolina', 'South Carolina', 'Georgia', 'Florida', 'Alabama',
          'Mississippi', 'Louisiana', 'Texas', 'California', 'Oregon',
          'Washington', 'Alaska', 'Hawaii')

# check if coastal or not
data$coastal = factor(ifelse(data$state %in% coast, 'yes', 'no'))
table(data$coastal) # 27 no, 23 yes

# population density (1975 population)
idx = match(data$state, state.name)
data$pop_density = state.x77[idx, 'Population'] * 1000 / state.x77[idx, 'Area']
sum(is.na(data$pop_density)) # 0

# summary of the new columns
summary(data[c('pre_trend', 'pop_density')])

From this we can see that 23 states are coastal and 27 are not. All 50 states matched the population data. The pre-war trend is positive for every state, from $0.24 to $0.76, so prices were already rising before the war.

Data Summary

{r}
# summary stats
summary(data)

The dollar increase (increase column) runs from $0.68 to $1.05 with a mean of $0.81. The middle half of states fall between $0.76 and $0.84, so most states are close together. The percent increase (pct column) runs from 22.3% to 31.0% with a mean of 26.8%. Pre-war prices (gas_price_prewar_feb27) run from $2.54 to $4.52, and the mean ($3.03) is above the median ($2.90), which means a few expensive states pull the average up. Population density is off balance, with a mean of 149 and a median of 73.

Log of Population Density

{r}
# log of density to reduce the pull of very dense states
data$log_density = log(data$pop_density)

This makes a new column, log_density, that holds the natural log of each state’s population density. The original column stays the same. 

Before and After Taking the Log

{r}
# before the log
hist(data$pop_density, main = 'Population Density', 
     xlab = 'people per square mile')

# after the log
hist(data$log_density, main = 'Log of Population Density', 
     xlab = 'log of people per square mile')

Before the log, more than 30 of the 50 states are under 100 people per square mile and a few stretch out to 1,000. After the log, the values are more balanced around 4, with Alaska as the one low point. We use the log version so a few dense states do not dominate the model.

Check Pre-Trend Count

{r}
table(data$pre_trend)

20 of the 50 states have a pre-war trend of $0.30, and 30 states share three values ($0.28, $0.30, $0.38). 

Because so many states share the same value, the Jan. 8 prices look rounded or estimated. So include pre_trend as a candidate predictor and say in the report that its data quality is questionable.

Check Increase Count

{r}
# how many states share each increase value
table(data$increase)

The values are concentrated. 36 of the 50 states fall in the range $0.76 to $0.84.

Plots

Histogram of the Response

{r}
# histogram of the response
hist(data$increase,
     main = 'Gas Price Increase, Feb. 27 to Mar. 19',
     xlab = 'increase (dollars per gallon)')

About 35 of the 50 states had an increase between $0.75 and $0.85. A small group of states stretches out to $1.05, so the distribution leans to the right.

Increase vs. Pre-War Prices

{r}
# increase (response) against pre-war price (predictor)
plot(data$prewar, data$increase, pch = 16,
     main = 'Increase vs. Pre-War Price',
     xlab = 'pre-war price (dollars per gallon)',
     ylab = 'increase (dollars per gallon)')
abline(lm(increase ~ prewar, data = data), col = 'red', lty = 2)
cor(data$prewar, data$increase)

The relationship is positive and close to a straight line (r = 0.89). States that were more expensive pre-war had a larger dollar increase than states that were cheaper pre-war. Most states sit between $2.50 and $3.40, and only six are above $3.50. Those six have a large effect on the slope, so we will double check them for influence later.

Increase against Pre-War Trend

{r}
# increase against pre-war trend
plot(data$pre_trend, data$increase, pch = 16,
     main = 'Increase vs. Pre-War Trend',
     xlab = 'price change, Jan. 8 to Feb. 27 (dollars per gallon)',
     ylab = 'increase (dollars per gallon)')
abline(lm(increase ~ pre_trend, data = data), col = 'red', lty = 2)
cor(data$pre_trend, data$increase)

The relationship is positive and moderate (r = 0.59). States whose prices rose more before the war also tended to rise more after it began. The pattern is much looser than for pre-war price (r = 0.89). Many states share the same trend value of $0.30, which stacks them in a vertical line.

Increase vs. Population Density

{r}
# increase against log population density
plot(data$log_density, data$increase, pch = 16,
     main = 'Increase vs. Population Density',
     xlab = 'log of people per square mile',
     ylab = 'increase (dollars per gallon)')
abline(lm(increase ~ log_density, data = data), col = 'red', lty = 2)
cor(data$log_density, data$increase)

There is almost no linear relationship (r = 0.09). The fitted line is flat, so density alone does not explain the increase.

Increase by Region

{r}
# increase by region
boxplot(increase ~ region, data = data,
        main = 'Gas Price Increase by Region',
        xlab = 'region',
        ylab = 'increase (dollars per gallon)')

The West has the highest median increase (about $0.85) and the widest spread, from $0.76 to $1.05. The Northeast is next (about $0.82) and is tightly grouped. The Midwest and South are lowest (about $0.76). The spread is not the same across regions, so we will test for equal variance before trusting the ANOVA.

Increase by Coastal Access

{r}
# increase by coastal
boxplot(increase ~ coastal, data = data,
        main = 'Gas Price Increase by Coastal Access',
        xlab = 'coastal state',
        ylab = 'increase (dollars per gallon)')

The medians are close ($0.80 for coastal, $0.78 for non-coastal) and the boxes overlap.

Correlations

{r}
# how the number predictors relate to each other
nums = c('increase', 'prewar', 'pre_trend', 'log_density')
round(cor(data[nums]), 2)

Pre-war price has the strongest correlation with the increase (0.89), followed by pre-war trend (0.59). Log density is close to zero (0.09). Pre-war price and pre-war trend are highly correlated with each other (0.82), so they carry overlapping information.

Sort the Data

{r}
# states with the largest increases
head(data[order(-data$increase), c('state', 'region', 'prewar', 'pre_trend', 'increase')])

# states with the smallest pre-war trend
head(data[order(data$pre_trend), c('state', 'pre_trend', 'increase')])

# states with the largest pre-war trend
head(data[order(-data$pre_trend), c('state', 'pre_trend', 'increase')])

# state with the lowest population density
data[which.min(data$pop_density), c('state', 'pop_density')]

Largest increases

The five largest increases are all in the West: Hawaii ($1.05), California ($1.01), Washington ($0.97), Nevada ($0.94), and Oregon ($0.88). These are also the five states with the highest pre-war prices, all above $3.70. Kentucky ties Oregon at $0.88 but had a pre-war price of only $2.84, so its increase is high for a cheap state.

Smallest pre-war trend

Hawaii had the smallest price change before the war ($0.24) but the largest increase after it began ($1.05), so it goes against the overall pattern. The other states with small trends (Oklahoma, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Texas) had small increases, between $0.69 and $0.78.

Largest pre-war trend

Washington ($0.76), California ($0.64), Oregon ($0.60), and Nevada ($0.54) had the largest price changes before the war, and all four had large increases after. These four West Coast area states are the points on the right side of the trend plot.

Lowest population density

Alaska has the lowest density at 0.64 people per square mile. It is the single low point on the log density histogram.

Overall takeaway

The same small group of Western states (Hawaii, California, Washington, Nevada, Oregon) sits at the extreme end of the increase, the pre-war price, and mostly the pre-war trend. They will have a large effect on any regression line, so they are the first states to look at in the influence checks. Kentucky and Hawaii are the two states that do not fit the general pattern.

Models

Linear Regression of Increase ~ Prewar

{r}
# fit the model
fit = lm(increase ~ prewar, data = data)
summary(fit)

# 95% confidence interval for the slope
confint(fit, 'prewar', level = 0.95) # (0.1305013, 0.1757117)

# t test for the slope
b1 = coef(summary(fit))['prewar', 'Estimate']
se = coef(summary(fit))['prewar', 'Std. Error']
df = df.residual(fit) # 48
t_stat = (b1 - 0) / se # test statistic
t_crit = qt(0.975, df = df) # critical value for a two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
p_val = 2 * pt(abs(t_stat), df = df, lower.tail = FALSE) # two-sided p value

t_stat # 13.61817
t_crit # 2.010635
p_val # 4.166268e-18

# anova table and critical value for the f test
anova(fit)
qf(0.95, 1, 48) # 4.042652

Regression function: The estimated regression function is $\hat{Y} = 0.3423 + 0.1531X$, where X is the pre-war price and Y is the increase. Each additional dollar of pre-war price is associated with about a $0.15 larger increase.

t test for the slope: We test $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ against $H_a: \beta_1 \neq 0$ at $\alpha = 0.05$. The decision rule is to reject $H_0$ if |t| > t(0.975, 48) = 2.0106. The test statistic is t = 13.618 with a p-value of 4.17e-18. Since 13.618 > 2.0106 and the p-value is less than 0.05, we reject null. There is strong evidence of a linear relationship between pre-war price and the increase.

Confidence interval for the slope: By hand, the 95% confidence interval is 0.1531 $\pm$ (2.0106 × 0.0112) = (0.1305, 0.1757). We are 95% confident that each additional dollar of pre-war price goes with an increase between $0.13 and $0.18 larger. The interval does not contain 0, which agrees with the t test.

F test: The ANOVA table gives F = 185.45. The decision rule is to reject $H_0$ if F > F(0.95, 1, 48) = 4.0427. Since 185.45 > 4.0427, we reject null and reach the same conclusion as the t test. The two tests always agree for a single predictor, since $13.618^2$ = 185.45.

Linear Regression of Percent Increase ~ Prewar

{r}
# fit the model with percent increase as the response
fit_pct = lm(pct ~ prewar, data = data)
summary(fit_pct)

# 95% confidence interval for the slope
confint(fit_pct, 'prewar', level = 0.95) # (-3.854509, -2.387518)

# t test for the slope
b1 = coef(summary(fit_pct))['prewar', 'Estimate']
se = coef(summary(fit_pct))['prewar', 'Std. Error']
df = df.residual(fit_pct) # 48
t_stat = (b1 - 0) / se # test statistic
t_crit = qt(0.975, df = df) # critical value for a two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
p_val = 2 * pt(abs(t_stat), df = df, lower.tail = FALSE) # two-sided p value

t_stat # -8.555223
t_crit # 2.010635
p_val # 3.231939e-11

# anova table and critical value for the f test
anova(fit_pct)
qf(0.95, 1, 48) # 4.042652

Regression function: The estimated regression function is $\hat{Y} = 36.2447 - 3.1210X$, where X is the pre-war price and Y is the percent increase. Each additional dollar of pre-war price is associated with a percent increase about 3.12 percentage points lower.

t test for the slope: We test $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ against $H_a: \beta_1 \neq 0$ at $\alpha = 0.05$. The decision rule is to reject $H_0$ if |t| > t(0.975, 48) = 2.0106. The test statistic is t = -8.555 with a p-value of 3.23e-11. Since |t| = 8.555 > 2.0106 and the p-value is less than 0.05, we reject null. There is strong evidence of a negative linear relationship between pre-war price and the percent increase.

Confidence interval for the slope: By hand, the 95% confidence interval is -3.1210 $\pm$ (2.0106 × 0.3648) = (-3.8545, -2.3875). We are 95% confident that each additional dollar of pre-war price goes with a percent increase between 2.39 and 3.85 percentage points lower. The interval does not contain 0, which agrees with the t test.

F test: The ANOVA table gives F = 73.192. The decision rule is to reject $H_0$ if F > F(0.95, 1, 48) = 4.0427. Since 73.192 > 4.0427, we reject null and reach the same conclusion as the t test, since $(-8.555)^2$ = 73.19.

Coefficient of determination: $R^2$ = 0.6039, so pre-war price explains about 60% of the variation in the percent increase. This is lower than the 79% in the dollar model.

Comparing the two models: The two slopes have opposite signs. States that were more expensive before the war had larger increases in dollars but smaller increases in percent. The dollar model explains why: the increase is about a flat $0.34 plus 15% of the pre-war price, and that flat amount is a larger share of a cheap state’s price than of an expensive state’s price.

ANOVA + Brown-Forsythe + Tukey

{r}
# mean increase by region
aggregate(increase ~ region, data = data, FUN = mean)

# single factor anova of the increase by region
fit_aov = aov(increase ~ region, data = data)
summary(fit_aov)

# critical value for the f test
qf(0.95, 3, 46) # 2.806845

# brown-forsythe test for equal variance across regions
levene.test(data$increase, data$region, location = 'median')

# tukey comparisons between pairs of regions
TukeyHSD(fit_aov)

Region means: The mean increase is $0.76 in the Midwest, $0.77 in the South, $0.82 in the Northeast, and $0.87 in the West.

F test for equality of region means: We test $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \mu_3 = \mu_4$ against $H_a$: not all $\mu_i$ are equal, at $\alpha = 0.05$. The decision rule is to reject null if F > F(0.95; 3, 46) = 2.8068. The test statistic is F = 9.265 with a p-value of 6.63e-05. Since 9.265 > 2.8068 and the p-value is less than 0.05, we reject null. There is strong evidence that the mean increase is not the same in all four regions.

Brown-Forsythe test for equal variance: We test $H_0$: the error variance is the same in all four regions against $H_a$: the error variance is not the same. The test statistic is 5.4465 with a p-value of 0.0027. Since the p-value is less than 0.05, we reject null. The spread of the increase differs by region, so the equal variance assumption of the ANOVA is not met. So the F test above should be read with caution.

Tukey comparisons: At a 95% family confidence level, two pairs of regions differ. The West is higher than the Midwest by $0.11 (interval $0.05 to $0.17, p = 0.0001) and higher than the South by $0.10 (interval $0.04 to $0.16, p = 0.0005). The other four intervals contain 0, so those pairs are not significantly different. The Northeast does not differ significantly from any other region. These intervals also rely on equal variance, so they carry the same caution.

Conclusion: Gas prices rose more in the West than in the Midwest and South.

Welch’s F test

{r}
# f test that does not assume equal variance
oneway.test(increase ~ region, data = data, var.equal = FALSE)

Because the equal variance assumption was not met, we repeated the test with Welch’s F test, which does not assume equal variance. It gives F = 9.409 with a p-value of 0.0003. Since the p-value is less than 0.05, we again reject null. The conclusion that the regions differ does not depend on the equal variance assumption.
